Lecture 9 The Binomial Distribution, Its Mean and Variance, and Sampling Without Replacement

How the binomial pmf comes out of a tree diagram, how to use it by hand and on the TI-84, why the mean is np and the variance np(1 − p), and when sampling without replacement can be treated as binomial.

1Binomial random variables

Binomial Random Variables

The heading is underlined on the board.

Definition

If you run a simple experiment times, and each run of the experiment has two possible [outcomes], then as as long successive trials are independent and the probability of one of the outcomes does not change, the random variable that counts the number of times one outcome occurs is called a binomial random variable.

“[outcomes]” is not on the board: the sentence ends at “two possible,”. The words “one outcome” near the end have a smudged line through them, as if partly wiped; they still read as “one outcome”. A student’s head is in the bottom left of the photo.

Notation

We usually let denote the number of trials and let denote the probability the outcome we we counting occurs on any given trial.

We will use the notation

to indicate is a binomial random variable with parameters and .

We often call the outcome we are counting a successful outcome and the other outcome a failure or nonsuccessful outcome.

Explanation (added) ✎

Board slips. “the outcome we we counting” should read “the outcome we are counting”, and “then as as long” has a doubled “as”. Neither changes the meaning.

The definition packs in four conditions, and a question is binomial only if all four hold: (1) a fixed number of trials, decided in advance; (2) each trial has two outcomes, success or failure; (3) the trials are independent; (4) the success probability is the same on every trial. is then the number of successes, so its possible values are . Condition (3) is the one that fails when you sample without replacement, which is where the lecture ends up in Section 8.

Textbook Devore §3.4, p. 117 lists the four conditions; p. 118 calls an experiment meeting them a binomial experiment (Definition); p. 119 defines the binomial random variable as the number of S’s and introduces . The board folds the experiment and the count into one definition.

3Example: drawing hearts with replacement

Example

You plan on selecting a single card with replacement from a standard deck of 52 playing cards 3 times. Each time you select a card, you will note whether or not it is a heart, place it back in the deck, and then shuffle properly.

If counts the number of hearts we get, then is a binomial variable with parameters and .

Explanation (added) ✎

Check the four conditions: draws fixed in advance; each draw is “heart” (success) or “not a heart” (failure); putting the card back and shuffling makes the draws independent; and every draw has because the deck is full each time. Without the replacement step the second and third probabilities would change (12/51 or 13/51), which is exactly the issue in Section 8.

How do we find , the pmf for ?

Lets use a tree diagram and just focus on .

S: Success, we draw a heart; F: Failure, we don’t draw a heart.

There are 3 outcomes that lead to getting 2 hearts,

Explanation (added) ✎

The tree has leaves, one per sequence of S and F. Multiplying along a path uses the multiplication rule for independent events from Lecture 6. The eight path probabilities are , which add to , as they must.

Same values just in a different order

A pair of small ditto-like marks to the right of the fourth line are not part of the working.

tells us the number of paths through the tree that correspond to getting 2 hearts.

On any one of theses paths, two of the edges will have a probability label of and the remaining edge will have a probability label of .

The probability of taking any specific one of these paths is .

The probability we end up taking one of the three is .

Explanation (added) ✎

Numerically: . The three paths are mutually exclusive because you can only follow one sequence of draws, so Axiom 3 (Lecture 3) lets you add.

Why counts the paths: a path with 2 hearts is decided by which 2 of the 3 draws are hearts. Choosing 2 positions out of 3 is a combination (Lecture 5), and , matching SSF, SFS, FSS. That idea is what makes the general formula in the next section work without drawing a tree.

Textbook Devore §3.4, p. 120, Table 3.1 lists all 16 outcomes for with their probabilities, the book’s version of this tree; is the same “number of sequences times the probability of one” idea.

4The binomial pmf

Theorem The binomial pmf

✱ If is a binomial random variable with parameters and ,

then

is the number of paths that correspond to to exactly succesful outcomes (and failures).

On any one of these paths, edges will have a probability label of .

The remaining edges will have a probability label of .

The probability we take a specific path with successes is .

Since there are of these paths and we can’t take more than one at the same time (mutually exclusive), the probability we take one of these paths is the sum of the probabilities which is

Lets construct the probability distribution table for , the binomial random variable from the previous example where we counted the number of times we selected a heart.

Explanation (added) ✎

This is the hearts calculation with the numbers replaced by letters: “2 hearts” becomes “ successes”, becomes , becomes , and becomes . The order of the S’s and F’s along a path does not change the product, only how many of each there are, which is why every path with successes has the same probability.

6Example: 1000 coin flips

Example

You plan on flipping a fair coin 1000 times. What is the probability you get between 400 and 500 heads (inclusively)?

You can use technology.

The exponent is written small; it reads as , which matches the calculator value . The left edge of the photo shows the end of the table from the previous board.

Explanation (added) ✎

“Inclusively” means 400 and 500 both count. includes everything from 0 to 500, so you subtract everything up to 399, not up to 400. This is the rule from Lecture 7, with .

TI-84: binomcdf(1000,0.5,500) − binomcdf(1000,0.5,399). The second value shows as 9.008412706E-11; the calculator writes “E-11” for .

Why the numbers look like that: the mean is and the standard deviation is (Section 7). 400 is about standard deviations below the mean, so getting 399 or fewer heads is almost impossible. And is a little more than because it includes and the distribution is symmetric about 500: .

8Sampling without replacement

Sampling without replacement

If you sample without replacement, the probability, the probability of selecting a population member changes from one selection to the next.

Definition

If counts the number of population members selected with this property, then is a hypergeometric random variable and not a binomial random variable.

Explanation (added) ✎

Board slip. “the probability, the probability” is a restart; read it once.

Without replacement, each draw changes what is left, so the draws are not independent and is not constant: two of the four binomial conditions fail. This is the same situation as Lecture 6’s sampling without replacement, where the conditional probability on each branch of the tree changed. The hypergeometric distribution is the exact model; the binomial is an approximation that is good when the population is big compared with the sample.

Textbook Devore §3.4, p. 118, Example 3.29: “if sampling is without replacement, the experiment will not yield independent trials.” The hypergeometric distribution is §3.5, p. 126, where the three assumptions are a population of , successes, and every subset of size equally likely.

9Example: brown hair, sampled without replacement

Even though is not a binomial random variable, we often treat it like one as long as the probability of selecting a population member with a given a property does not change very much between selections.

Explanation (added) ✎

Board slip. “with a given a property” should be “with a given property”.

“Does not change very much” is made precise by the example that follows and by the 5% cut-off in Section 10.

Example

In a population of 10000 people, 4000 have brown hair. Suppose we select 20 people without replacement, and at each step, all remaining people are equally likely to be selected.

⋮

(most extreme cases)

The instructor’s arm is in the bottom left of image 22.

Explanation (added) ✎

Where 3981 and 9981 come from: after 19 people are removed, remain. If all 19 had brown hair, brown-haired people are left. If none did, all 4000 are left. These are the two ends; every other history gives something in between. Rounded to three decimals: and .

Textbook Devore §3.4, p. 119, Example 3.29 makes the same argument with a jury pool of 500,000 (400,000 employed) and a sample of 10: the tenth pick is 0.799996 or 0.800014 at the extremes, so it is treated as .

Since the probability of selecting a brown haired person does not change very much, we can pretend the probability is always (like when we sample with replacement) and get good approximations to the probabilities.

We can treat like a binomial random variable.

Lets estimate the probability we get 5 brown haired people in our selection of 20 people.

Explanation (added) ✎

Board slip. The exact value is , not 0.07465. The board repeated the binomial answer from the previous board here. The instructor’s own comparison table in Section 10 has the exact value as 0.07457.

Why the formula works: this is classical probability, from Lecture 4. Every group of 20 people is equally likely, and there are groups. A group with exactly brown-haired people is made by choosing of the 4000 brown-haired people and of the other 6000, so there are of them (multiplication rule for counting). No tree is needed.

Comparison Table

Binomial Approx

The instructor is holding a sheet of paper in front of the board at the right; it covers nothing in the table.

Rule

✱ The smaller the sample size is in relation to the population size, the better the better the estimates will be.

Cut-off Only do this when the sample size is at most 5% of the population size.

Explanation (added) ✎

Board slip. “the better the better” is a repeated phrase; it means “the better the estimates will be”. The boxed inequality is a restatement of the cut-off, not written on the board.

Here , far under 5%, and the table shows the binomial answers agree with the exact ones to about 3 decimal places; the largest gap in the typed table is 0.00018 at . Relative to their size, the far tails disagree a little more (: vs , about 3%), but those probabilities are so small that it never matters.

This is the 5% rule from Lecture 6, now with a reason behind it: with a small sample, removing a few people barely changes the proportion left (Section 9), so the draws are nearly independent with nearly constant . The second widget below lets you push the sample past 5% and watch the two distributions separate.

Textbook examples worth reading

  • Example 3.29, pp. 118–119. Picking 6 jurors from a pool of 50 is not binomial because the chance of “employed” changes with each pick (0.667 vs 0.778 on the sixth). With a pool of 500,000 the changes are tiny, so it is treated as . This is the brown-hair argument.
  • Example 3.30, p. 121. Six cola drinkers with no preference: , with , “at least three” and “at most one” worked out.
  • Example 3.31, pp. 121–122. Textbook binding failures, : exactly, at most, at least and between-inclusive probabilities from the cdf. Part 4 points out that uses the row, not the row, as in the 1000-flip example.
  • Example 3.33, p. 123. Credit-card purchases, : , , , and the chance lands within one standard deviation of its mean.
  • Example 3.34, p. 126. Choosing 5 of 20 printer service orders (12 inkjet): counted the same way as the brown-hair exact formula.

Worked question §3.4 #57, p. 124 ✎

Ten flashlights each need two type-D batteries, and a flashlight works only if both batteries are acceptable. 90% of batteries are acceptable. Find the probability that at least nine of the ten flashlights work.

Try it first, then open

The trick is that the trial is a flashlight, not a battery. Assuming batteries are acceptable independently of each other,

Assuming the flashlights are independent, the number that work is .

TI-84: 1 − binomcdf(10,0.81,8) → 0.4067564617. (Checked in code.)

Assumptions used: batteries are acceptable independently of each other (so both are good with probability ), and the ten flashlights work independently with the same probability (so the count is binomial).

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Decide whether a situation is binomial (check the four conditions) and state and , as in the hearts and coin examples.
  • Find with , showing the setup, then confirm with binompdf.
  • Find “at most”, “at least” or “between, inclusive” probabilities as differences of cdf values, as in the 1000-flip example.
  • Build the full distribution table for a small (like ) and check that it adds to 1.
  • Find , and for a binomial; possibly derive and from Bernoulli variables.
  • Sampling without replacement: compute the exact probability with combinations, decide by the 5% rule whether the binomial approximation is allowed, and compare the two.
